topic.title: Node.js — Quick Revision
topic.subtitle: The runtime concepts that come up in backend and full-stack interviews.

questions.q: What is Node.js and why is it fast for I/O?

answer.value: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine. It uses a **single-threaded event loop** with non-blocking I/O (libuv), so one process can handle many concurrent connections while waiting on disk or network.

questions.q: Explain the Node.js event loop phases.

items: **timers** — `setTimeout`/`setInterval` callbacks
**pending callbacks** — deferred system callbacks
**poll** — retrieve and run I/O callbacks
**check** — `setImmediate` callbacks
**close callbacks**

answer.value: `process.nextTick` and promise microtasks run between phases, before the loop continues.

items: `nextTick` — runs right after the current operation, before other async work.
`setTimeout(0)` — timers phase, after at least ~1 ms.
`setImmediate` — check phase, after I/O callbacks.
CommonJS: `require()` / `module.exports`, synchronous loading.
ESM: `import` / `export`, static analysis and top-level `await`; enable with `"type": "module"` or `.mjs`.

questions.q: How do callbacks, promises and async/await relate in Node?

answer.value: Callbacks (error-first `(err, data)`) came first and led to nesting. Promises flatten chains and `async/await` makes them read like sync code. `util.promisify` or `fs/promises` convert callback APIs.

import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
const text = await readFile('data.json', 'utf8');

A function `(req, res, next)` that runs between the request and the final handler — for logging, parsing bodies, authentication, validation, error handling. Order matters; call `next()` to continue or end the response.

questions.q: How do you handle errors in Node/Express?

items: Use `try/catch` with `async/await` and pass errors to `next(err)`.
Register an error-handling middleware `(err, req, res, next)` last.
Listen for `unhandledRejection` / `uncaughtException` to log and exit cleanly.

questions.q: What are streams and why use them?

answer.value: Streams process data in chunks instead of loading it all in memory — `Readable`, `Writable`, `Duplex`, `Transform`. They give low memory use and backpressure handling.

questions.q: What is the difference between fork, spawn, worker threads and cluster?

items: `child_process.spawn/fork` start separate OS processes.
`worker_threads` run JS on extra threads within one process — good for CPU-heavy work.
`cluster` forks one worker per CPU core sharing a server port.

questions.q: How do you secure a Node API?

items: Validate and sanitise all input; use parameterised queries.
Hash passwords (bcrypt/argon2); use short-lived JWTs or sessions with `HttpOnly` cookies.
`helmet` headers, CORS allow-list, rate limiting.
Keep dependencies updated; never commit secrets — use environment variables.

questions.q: What is package.json and the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?

answer.value: `package.json` describes the project: name, scripts, and dependencies. `dependencies` are needed at runtime; `devDependencies` only for development (tests, linters, build tools). `package-lock.json` pins exact versions.
A fixed-size chunk of raw binary memory outside the V8 heap, used for files, network packets and encodings.

questions.q: What is the difference between REST and GraphQL?

answer.value: REST exposes multiple resource endpoints with fixed responses. GraphQL exposes one endpoint where the client specifies exactly the fields it needs, reducing over- and under-fetching at the cost of more server complexity.

questions.q: How do you scale a Node.js application?

items: Run multiple processes (cluster/PM2) or containers behind a load balancer.
Keep the app stateless; move sessions to Redis.
Cache hot data, use queues for slow jobs, offload CPU work to worker threads.
